newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader cracks down on hostage-takers.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader cracks down on hostage-takers.

text.p: Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov, keen to improve his image and assert full control over his breakaway Russian region, launched an operation on Monday to clamp down on hostage-taking groups.

Interfax news agency said Operation Shield of Law, coordinated by the special anti-terrorist service, would aim especially at securing the release of five Russian reporters whose abduction has complicated the uneasy ties between Russia and Chechnya.

It said police were combing the Chechen capital Grozny and other parts of the southern region for a three-member crew of Russia's commercial NTV television and two journalists from the Vzglyad news programme.
Taking hostages for ransom has become widespread in Chechnya, which was devastated by Russia's ill-fated 1994-96 military campaign to crush its independence drive.
Earlier this month, Chechen security forces won the release of a separate group of three Russian reporters, an Austrian businessman and a local resident held hostage by unidentified armed groups.

The rash of kidnapping prompted speculation in Moscow that Maskhadov, who won presidential polls in January after Moscow and Grozny had concluded a peace deal, was not in full control of his Caucasian territory.

Maskhadov denies such suggestions but has recently taken some steps clearly aimed at asserting his personal control and neutralising potential threats from influential field commanders backed by powerful clans.
On Sunday he signed a decree dissolving the elite commando regiment Borz (Wolf), one of the most prominent combat forces during the 21-month conflict with Russian troops that ended last August.

"The leadership of the regiment has taken the path of illegal actions," Interfax quoted Maskhadov's decree as saying. "Some of its servicemen have been charged with criminal offences including hostage-taking and other outrages.
"The regiment has launched unsanctioned raids and has set up unsanctioned road posts to extort money from passing cars."

Another decree issued on Sunday banned the self-styled army of field commander Salman Raduyev, who has openly challenged Maskhadov's authority and has complicated negotiations with Moscow by threatening terrorist actions in Russian cities.
Maskhadov, who led Chechnya's guerrilla army against Russian troops and then played a key role in the peace talks, is now trying to map out a long-term relationship with Moscow.

Under the peace deal, Russia has withdrawn its forces from Chechnya in exchange for a rebel promise to put off until 2001 a decision on whether the region should become independent -- the issue at the heart of their conflict.

Russia has ruled out Chechen independence and hopes that by 2001 it will have found ways to keep the region from seceding. Grozny sees the postponement as a chance to win better conditions in what it sees as an inevitable divorce.
Moscow and Grozny are now discussing control of a pipeline that runs across Chechnya and will deliver oil from Azerbaijan's new rich off-shore deposits to Black Sea ports.
To boost his negotiating position, Maskhadov needs to show he has enough control over Chechnya to ensure the safety of the pipeline.
